doc.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Learning repertoire from the radio and practicing melodies solo
summary: He and Bucky Pizzarelli learned standards from the radio; he now practices by playing and accompanying melodies like Donna Lee on solo bass.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: No. So when you got into the bass, what did you feel, in addition to learning to physically play it and get that part down, the technique, did you then realize that there was a whole repertory of tunes that you had to get into? And how did you go about that?

Boy I was speaking to Bucky Pizzarelli about this yesterday. He and I were of a generation, we never sat down and learned music. We heard it on the radio. We heard all the songs on the radio that anybody ever played. They were the pop songs of the day that became the jazz standards of later on. And I never sat down and studied a song. I’d always heard it on the radio. I mean well I might write out some substitute changes for it, but I heard so much jazz and you heard so many versions of it, that you knew 27 different substitutes for every song anyway. I rarely sat down and studied songs. Because I’d heard them all. Most people did pop songs, then of course when people started writing jazz songs, which in the bop era they started really writing, well I guess before that, but as far as I was concerned that’s when they really started writing, bop. But even then you heard, somehow you heard those. Okay. And a bass player didn’t have to study the leads to these things, which I now spend much more time doing, because as a solo player to be able to walk up and be able to do a solo version of a Charlie Parker song on just bass and try to make it interesting, it’s great practice, I mean that’s the way I practice now is to do that.

Play the melody and then try to accompany the melody. Like [scats], you know and take like “Donna Lee” and tear it apart. Don’t just play the melody, but also accompany it and try to find ways to make it interesting on the bass. Meanwhile you’re using your ear and you’re solving all kinds of problems and melodic intervals and things, and playing melodies is good because you’re forced to play stuff that you wouldn’t think of in a solo situation on the bass. You know, solo-wise you’re going to play something that you can play. But all of a sudden you’ve got to play the melody and you’re forced into learning other things. But I don’t want to play classical melodies, because I’m not going to use them. Unless they’re really fascinating to me, I’d rather play something that I really want to hear. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-
So like “All the Things You Are,” tunes like that, the stuff from The Real Book, or the third of it that people really play, those tunes were being played on the radio by artists —

Oh you heard them constantly. I mean don’t forget, pop radio in those days, in the ‘40’s and ‘50s, this was, I mean in the ‘40s, all it was was big bands and maybe some corny pop songs. I don’t want to put anybody down but like Rosie Clooney’s a good friend of mine, but her “Come Ona My House” songs in that category, which seemed to be the pop. But in spite of that there was all these wonderful songs from Broadway and the standards, and Irving Berlin and Porter and everybody. That’s all you heard on the radio. And you got to know those songs inherently. So The Real Book, you look at it, you laugh. I mean you grew up hearing those songs. So that’s what I don’t envy about guys who have to, these days they’ve got to sit and really work to get the music. But then they become very well rounded because now they’re into all the styles of music too. They’re hearing all the music of the day. I mean jazz is always evolving hopefully, and changing.
